paragraphs: Scaling laws describe how model performance changes as training data and model capacity grow. This paper asks how those relationships change when training collections increasingly contain material generated by other models. Its central concern is whether the patterns used to predict progress from human or natural data still apply when synthetic data enters the process.

The authors develop a theoretical framework that describes model collapse through changes in scaling behavior. They analyze several outcomes: improvements can stop following their previous scaling pattern, scaling can shift across successive model generations, and previously acquired skills can be lost. They also study grokking when human and synthesized data are mixed, showing that their framework covers more than a single pattern of deterioration.

The theory is supported by large-scale experiments involving a transformer on arithmetic and Llama2 for text generation. The findings frame collapse as a range of changes in learning behavior, rather than establishing that every use of synthetic data inevitably produces complete failure.
icml-2024-a-tale-of-tails-model-collapse.tldr: The paper explains model collapse through changes in scaling laws, revealing several ways synthetic training data can alter learning and skill retention.

paragraphs: Training with low-bit integers reduces the numerical precision used for weights, activations, and gradients. This can reduce computational demands, but choosing how much precision each component needs is difficult. The paper introduces AMPA, a framework that adaptively assigns mixed precision across all three components and supports precision below the commonly used INT8 level.

AMPA uses a magnitude-based sensitivity measure built from quantization losses and average gradient magnitudes. The authors show theoretically that this measure upper-bounds the influence of quantization. They also design a strategy for updating precision layer by layer, using observations about quantization losses and their effects on model performance during low-bit training.

Experiments across different network backbones and datasets cover image classification, image segmentation, and language modeling. Compared with INT8 quantization, the method achieves more than a 38% reduction in BitOPs with reported performance loss below 2%. These findings support adaptive precision as a way to reduce the bit-level computation required for training while controlling the accompanying performance tradeoff.
icml-2024-ampa-adaptive-mixed-precision-.tldr: AMPA adaptively allocates low-bit precision during training, reducing BitOPs by more than 38% versus INT8 with reported performance loss below 2%.

paragraphs: Determining which of two variables causes the other is difficult when competing causal structures are Markov equivalent. Much existing work seeks assumptions strong enough to guarantee that the direction can be identified. This paper argues that those assumptions can restrict applicability and instead places causal assumptions inside a Bayesian framework.

The resulting task is Bayesian model selection: compare models representing different causal directions using the assumptions built into them. The authors explain why this approach can distinguish structures in situations where maximum-likelihood methods fail. The distinction matters because fitting the observed distribution well does not, by itself, settle which causal direction should be preferred.

To demonstrate the approach, the paper constructs a Bayesian non-parametric model that flexibly represents the joint distribution of the variables. It outperforms previous methods across benchmark datasets with varied data-generating assumptions. The contribution is a way to reason about causal direction through explicit Bayesian modeling, with empirical evidence across different settings, rather than a claim that causal direction can be recovered without assumptions.
icml-2024-bivariate-causal-discovery-usi.tldr: Bayesian model selection incorporates causal assumptions to distinguish competing causal directions and improves results across varied benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Adversarially robust classification asks whether predictions remain correct when inputs are deliberately perturbed. Strong statistical guarantees are known under restrictive distributional models, but much less is established without those models. This paper studies binary linear classification in a non-parametric setting, assuming only mild regularity of the feature distribution conditional on the class.

The authors introduce an estimator that minimizes a sequence of smoothed versions of the robust 0/1 loss. Its smoothing bandwidth changes with both the number of observations and the number of dimensions. Their analysis accommodates attacks measured using arbitrary norms and proves consistency with respect to adversarial risk under the stated conditions.

The estimator can also attain the minimax excess adversarial risk rate of roughly the square root of dimension divided by sample size, up to logarithmic factors. Achieving that rate may require solving rougher optimization problems. The result therefore connects statistical robustness under weaker distributional assumptions with a concrete optimization tradeoff, rather than transferring the faster rates available under strong parametric assumptions.
icml-2024-consistent-adversarially-robus.tldr: A progressively smoothed estimator achieves consistent adversarially robust linear classification under mild distributional conditions, with an optimal rate available at an optimization cost.

paragraphs: Learning an understandable policy from observed decisions becomes difficult when the same decision rule is expected to explain every context. This paper proposes Contextualized Policy Recovery, or CPR, to represent complex decision-making through many simpler policies. It treats each context as a separate task within a shared multi-task learning framework.

Each context-specific policy is a linear map, and CPR generates updated policy models as new observations change the context. This lets the overall decision process vary while keeping its individual components intelligible. The authors provide two versions: one offers exact local interpretability, while the other retains full global interpretability.

Studies on simulated and real data include predicting antibiotic prescriptions in intensive care and MRI prescriptions for Alzheimer’s patients. The reported AUROC improvements over the previous state of the art are 22% and 7.7%, respectively. In these evaluations, CPR closes the accuracy gap between interpretable and black-box approaches. The resulting models support detailed examination of context-specific prescribing decisions, rather than requiring one universal policy to account for all observed behavior.
icml-2024-contextualized-policy-recovery.tldr: CPR models medical decisions with adaptive, context-specific linear policies, improving prescription prediction while preserving local or global interpretability.

paragraphs: Neural-symbolic systems combine neural components with symbolic structure, making parameter learning depend on how inference is performed. This paper develops a general gradient-based learning framework using convex and bilevel optimization. It demonstrates the framework with NeuPSL, connecting the optimization used to produce predictions with the gradients needed to learn model parameters.

The authors introduce smooth primal and dual formulations of NeuPSL inference and show that learning gradients can be expressed using optimal dual variables. They then design a dual block coordinate descent algorithm that naturally uses warm starts. Reusing a previous solution gives the optimization procedure a useful starting point when solving subsequent inference problems during learning.

The paper reports learning runtime improvements exceeding 100 times relative to the current best NeuPSL inference method. Across eight datasets spanning different tasks, the learning framework also achieves prediction improvements of up to 16 percentage points over alternative learning methods. Together, these results show that reformulating inference can improve both the efficiency of parameter learning and the predictions obtained in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-convex-and-bilevel-optimizatio.tldr: A convex and bilevel optimization framework makes NeuPSL learning substantially faster and yields prediction gains of up to 16 percentage points.

paragraphs: Training Transformers with differential privacy presents obstacles beyond those encountered in ordinary neural networks. This paper takes a modular approach: address the difficulties specific to Transformers so that methods developed for more basic private neural-network training become applicable. The goal is to connect Transformer training to an existing body of model-agnostic techniques.

The authors identify two particular difficulties. One is an attention distraction phenomenon, which concerns the attention mechanism in private Transformer training. The other is incompatibility with existing methods for efficient gradient clipping. These are treated as distinct problems, allowing the proposed solutions to target separate parts of the training process.

The paper introduces Re-Attention to address attention distraction and Phantom Clipping to address the clipping issue. Its contribution is an approach to organizing private Transformer training around these specific obstacles and their corresponding remedies. The authors argue that this modular treatment can also help advance differentially private deep learning by making progress on general neural-network methods easier to carry over to Transformers.
icml-2024-delving-into-differentially-pr.tldr: Re-Attention and Phantom Clipping address two Transformer-specific obstacles to applying general differentially private training methods.

paragraphs: In decentralized optimization, agents train through communication with neighboring agents instead of relying on one central coordinator. The communication network can strongly affect how quickly their updates converge. This paper focuses on distributed stochastic gradient tracking, or DSGT, whose theoretical iteration complexity includes terms that depend on the network’s topology.

The authors introduce snap-shot DSGT and an accelerated version, called SS-DSGT and ASS-DSGT. Both use snap-shot gradient tracking to address the network-dependent behavior of the existing method. They establish a lower iteration complexity for SS-DSGT on general communication networks. For ASS-DSGT, they report a match to the stated DSGT iteration bound under the same conditions used for that comparison.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical motivation: SS-DSGT performs better on general network topologies, while ASS-DSGT shows better practical performance for the specified communication matrix. The contribution combines algorithm design with an analysis of how information exchange shapes convergence, giving distinct theoretical and empirical comparisons rather than one unconditional speedup claim for every network.
icml-2024-double-stochasticity-gazes-fas.tldr: Two snap-shot gradient-tracking methods improve decentralized optimization, with network-dependent theoretical guarantees and supporting numerical results.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization works with function evaluations rather than directly available gradients. In composite optimization, its random gradient estimates create coordinate-wise variance in addition to ordinary sampling variance. Earlier methods reduce this extra variability by estimating every partial derivative, requiring a number of function evaluations proportional to the dimension and making high-dimensional problems expensive.

The paper introduces Zeroth-order Proximal Double Variance Reduction, or ZPDVR. It uses an averaging technique to reduce both sources of variance while relying only on random gradient estimates. Each iteration requires a constant expected number of stochastic zeroth-order oracle calls, avoiding the need to estimate all partial derivatives at every step.

For the strongly convex and smooth setting, the authors establish an optimal total query complexity proportional to d(n + κ) log(1/ε), with κ denoting the condition number and ε the target accuracy. Dimension therefore still appears in the overall cost. Empirical results support linear convergence and show better performance than related methods, linking cheaper individual iterations with a strong total-computation guarantee.
icml-2024-double-variance-reduction-a-sm.tldr: ZPDVR reduces two sources of gradient-estimation variance, achieving optimal query complexity in the strongly convex, smooth setting with constant expected oracle calls per iteration.

paragraphs: Many clustering-style problems involve several candidate parameter choices, with each objective contribution taking the value of whichever choice fits it best. This paper formalizes that structure as sum-of-minimum optimization. The overall goal is to minimize the sum or average of these minimum values, providing a shared formulation for multiple machine-learning applications.

The authors design algorithms inspired by randomized initialization for k-means and by Lloyd’s algorithm. They extend these ideas beyond the classic clustering objective to the broader optimization model. Their analysis establishes a tight bound for the generalized initialization procedure and a convergence rate resembling gradient descent for the generalized Lloyd procedure.

Numerical evaluations cover generalized principal component analysis, mixed linear regression, and small-scale neural-network training. The methods compare favorably with previous approaches that use simpler but less precise reformulations. The significance is that the minimum-over-candidates structure can be handled directly within a common algorithmic framework, with theoretical guarantees and evidence across several tasks rather than a separate formulation for every application.
icml-2024-efficient-algorithms-for-sum-o.tldr: The paper generalizes k-means-style optimization to sums of minimum-valued objectives, with tight initialization analysis and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Co-training aims to learn from few labeled examples under suitable assumptions, but proving both label efficiency and computational efficiency has been difficult. This paper studies co-training in a stream-based active-learning setting, where examples arrive in a stream and the learner can selectively request labels. Its results use the standard weak-dependence assumption.

The main construction reduces this co-training problem to online classification. Consequently, any concept class that is efficiently learnable in the mistake-bound online model receives an efficient co-training algorithm whose label complexity is independent of the target error. This transfers useful guarantees from online learning into the co-training setting.

A broader reduction gives label complexity of approximately d log(1/ε) for classes with VC dimension d, but is not generally computationally efficient. Additional online-learning ideas yield efficient algorithms using approximately d² log(1/ε) labels for several classes, including unions of intervals and homogeneous halfspaces. The paper thus separates low label requirements from efficient computation and establishes settings where both can be achieved.
icml-2024-fast-co-training-under-weak-de.tldr: A reduction to online classification yields provably label-efficient and computationally efficient co-training algorithms for several concept classes under weak dependence.

paragraphs: Language-model training commonly joins documents together and cuts the resulting text into equal-length sequences. This avoids wasting space on padding, but it also splits many documents into incomplete fragments. The paper examines how those avoidable cuts interfere with learning content that is coherent, factually consistent, and grounded in the complete context.

The proposed method, Best-fit Packing, uses document lengths in a combinatorial optimization procedure to arrange documents into training sequences. The authors report that it eliminates unnecessary truncations while maintaining the training efficiency of concatenation. This makes the organization of training data itself the intervention, preserving more complete document context without giving up efficient sequence packing.

Experiments on text and code pre-training report gains of 4.7% in reading comprehension, 16.8% in context following, and 9.2% in program synthesis. Closed-domain hallucination is reduced by up to 58.3%. These results indicate that preserving document integrity during sequence construction can materially affect what a language model learns, even when the reported training efficiency remains the same.
icml-2024-fewer-truncations-improve-lang.tldr: Best-fit Packing preserves document context without sacrificing training efficiency, improving text and code performance and reducing closed-domain hallucination.

paragraphs: Diffusion image models are often understood as generalizing by combining factors learned from their training images. This paper investigates a different possibility: whether a model can generate intermediate values of an attribute even when those intermediate examples were absent during training. The authors train denoising diffusion probabilistic models on strictly separated parts of a data distribution.

The separation deliberately leaves large gaps in the values of the underlying factors represented in training. For example, a model sees clearly smiling faces and non-smiling faces, while the intermediate region is unexplored. The authors demonstrate a sampling procedure that generates slightly smiling faces without requiring reference images, which they describe as zero-shot interpolation.

They reproduce the finding for other attributes and datasets. The experiments therefore provide evidence that these models can reach intermediate regions of a distribution, extending the observed behavior beyond combining already represented factors. The result is a demonstrated capability under the studied training and sampling setup, rather than a guarantee that every missing region of any image distribution can be generated.
icml-2024-going-beyond-compositions-ddpm.tldr: Diffusion models trained on separated attribute ranges can generate unseen intermediate images through a sampling procedure that requires no reference images.

paragraphs: Optimization over Riemannian manifolds uses gradient methods in spaces with geometric structure. As in more familiar optimization settings, the learning rate strongly affects how quickly an algorithm converges. Choosing it can require careful manual tuning. This paper develops stochastic optimization algorithms for these spaces that remove the need to hand-tune the learning rate.

The theoretical contribution is a set of high-probability convergence guarantees. The authors compare these guarantees with the best-known optimally tuned rate in the deterministic setting and show optimality up to logarithmic factors. This comparison gives a precise sense in which removing manual learning-rate selection can coexist with a strong convergence guarantee, rather than relying solely on practical convenience.

Numerical experiments show competitive performance against algorithms that depend on a learning rate. The findings combine a reduction in tuning burden with theoretical support and empirical validation. The stated empirical outcome is competitive performance, while the theoretical comparison is specifically to the optimally tuned deterministic rate and allows logarithmic differences.
icml-2024-learning-rate-free-stochastic-.tldr: Learning-rate-free algorithms for Riemannian stochastic optimization provide high-probability convergence guarantees and competitive empirical performance without manual learning-rate tuning.

paragraphs: Decentralized multi-agent systems often have relationships that change as agents move or interact. This paper introduces the Locally Interdependent Multi-Agent MDP to study such changing dependencies theoretically. The framework can represent settings including cooperative navigation, obstacle avoidance, and formation control, where relevant interactions need not remain fixed over time.

General partially observable multi-agent problems can be intractable, but the authors exploit the structure of this setting to propose three closed-form policies. These policies have theoretical near-optimality guarantees and can be scalable to compute and store. The analysis also relates limited local visibility to the performance available when the entire system is observable.

Specifically, the decentralized, partially observable solution is exponentially close to the fully observable solution as a function of visibility radius within this framework. This quantifies how expanding local visibility narrows the performance gap. The paper also discusses extensions aimed at improving tractability and uses simulations to investigate long-horizon policy behavior, connecting the theoretical policies with their behavior over extended operation.
icml-2024-locally-interdependent-multi-a.tldr: A framework for locally interacting decentralized agents yields near-optimal policies and an exponentially shrinking gap to full observability as visibility grows.

paragraphs: Extending a language model’s context window is difficult because long-text fine-tuning is costly and new token positions can create problematic values. LongRoPE addresses these issues by changing positional embeddings while retaining the model’s original architecture. The paper reports extending pretrained models to a 2048k-token context using up to 1k fine-tuning steps at training lengths within 256k.

The method searches for two kinds of non-uniformity in positional interpolation. This improves the starting point for fine-tuning and also enables an eightfold extension without fine-tuning in the studied scenarios. A progressive procedure first fine-tunes a model at 256k context length, then applies another positional interpolation to reach 2048k.

LongRoPE additionally readjusts the model at an 8k length to recover short-context performance. Experiments with LLaMA2 and Mistral across various tasks support the approach’s effectiveness. Because the changes are concentrated in positional embeddings, the extended models can reuse most existing optimizations. The contribution combines very long context support with an explicit step to preserve performance at the original shorter window.
icml-2024-longrope-extending-llm-context.tldr: LongRoPE extends pretrained language models to 2048k-token contexts through searched positional interpolation and progressive extension while recovering short-context performance.

paragraphs: A confidence score is useful when it reflects how often an answer is actually correct. Calibration averaged over all answers can obscure differences between kinds of questions or responses. This paper applies multicalibration to language-model outputs, asking confidence scores to remain calibrated across multiple overlapping groups of prompt-and-completion pairs.

The authors construct groups in two ways. One clusters examples in an embedding space; the other asks the language model yes-or-no questions about the prompt, producing what they call self-annotations. These groupings are correlated with the probability that a response is correct. The paper also introduces multicalibration algorithm variants designed to reduce overfitting and thereby improve performance.

Benchmarking across several question-answering datasets and language models shows substantial improvements over existing methods in fine-grained measures of calibration and accuracy. The practical contribution is confidence scoring that accounts for differences within the data, rather than relying only on an overall average. The findings concern the measured reliability and accuracy of the proposed scoring techniques in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-multicalibration-for-confidenc.tldr: Multicalibration improves LLM confidence scores by calibrating them across overlapping groups formed through embeddings and model-generated prompt annotations.

paragraphs: Optimizing for average human preferences can be problematic when a task calls for many different good responses. Quality Diversity algorithms explicitly search for both quality and variety, but often require someone to design a diversity metric by hand. This paper proposes Quality Diversity through Human Feedback, or QDHF, to learn that metric from people instead.

QDHF progressively infers diversity measures from human judgments about the similarity of candidate solutions. This supplies the diversity information needed by Quality Diversity search without requiring a manually crafted measure. The approach is intended for complex, open-ended tasks where deciding what counts as a meaningful difference is itself part of the problem.

Experiments show that QDHF outperforms state-of-the-art automatic diversity-discovery methods and matches Quality Diversity approaches using handcrafted metrics on standard robotics and reinforcement-learning benchmarks. For diffusion-based text-to-image generation, it substantially improves diversity and receives more favorable user-study responses. The paper also analyzes scalability, robustness, and the quality of learned diversity metrics, examining how the feedback-derived measures support open-ended optimization.
icml-2024-quality-diversity-through-huma.tldr: QDHF learns diversity metrics from human similarity judgments, supporting high-quality varied solutions and improving diversity in text-to-image generation.

paragraphs: Graph models face a tension between capturing distant information and preserving the structure of the graph. Repeated one-hop message passing can struggle with distant nodes, while graph transformers allow direct interactions but rely on added positional information. This paper proposes an architecture that organizes long-range information using the graph’s own shortest-path distances.

For each target node, the model groups other nodes according to their distance from it and aggregates each group into a hop representation. A linear recurrent neural network then processes the resulting sequence. Its specially chosen diagonal parameterization supports stable propagation over long ranges, and the authors prove that it is expressive enough to encode the hierarchy of neighborhoods.

The model does not require positional encoding. Across several benchmarks, its measured performance matches or exceeds state-of-the-art graph transformers while using significantly less computation. The approach therefore provides an explicit way to combine distance-based graph structure with long-range sequence modeling, with theoretical support for representing neighborhood hierarchy and empirical support for its computational advantages.
icml-2024-recurrent-distance-filtering-f.tldr: A linear recurrent model processes distance-grouped graph neighborhoods, matching or exceeding graph-transformer performance on benchmarks with substantially lower computation.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation when the underlying Gaussian structure is sparse and some observations are contaminated under Huber’s model. It covers mean estimation, principal component analysis, and linear regression. The authors give estimators that are efficient in both sample use and computation while attaining optimal error guarantees within constant factors.

The mean-estimation result makes the improvement concrete. For a k-sparse mean in d dimensions and corruption rate ε, the estimator uses roughly k²/ε² samples multiplied by logarithmic factors in d/ε. It runs in time polynomial in the sample size and achieves Euclidean error O(ε). Previous efficient algorithms incur an additional square-root logarithmic factor in their error.

The technical contribution is a multidimensional filtering method designed for the sparse regime. It enables the stronger accuracy guarantee without abandoning computational efficiency. The authors suggest that the filtering technique may have further applications. The established results specifically concern the Gaussian sparse estimation tasks and contamination model analyzed, where prior efficient methods had quantitatively worse error guarantees.
icml-2024-robust-sparse-estimation-for-g.tldr: A sparse multidimensional filtering method yields efficient robust Gaussian estimators with error guarantees optimal up to constant factors.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer low energy use on neuromorphic hardware, but robustness remains a challenge. This paper studies robustness through the stability of nonlinear systems. It focuses on how perturbations affect the membrane potentials of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and how changing the neuron dynamics can help control those effects.

The authors simplify the dynamics governing membrane-potential perturbations and show that these dynamics reliably reflect perturbation intensity. Their theoretical analysis indicates that the simplified system satisfies input-output stability. This connects a description of how disturbances propagate inside the neurons with a mathematical property relevant to controlling their influence.

Using that analysis, the paper proposes a training framework with modified spiking neurons and an objective that reduces the mean squared membrane-potential perturbation. Image-classification experiments under Gaussian-noise training and adversarial training verify the framework’s effectiveness. The contribution is a stability-motivated route to improving robustness, supported by theory for the simplified dynamics and empirical evaluation of the resulting training approach.
icml-2024-robust-stable-spiking-neural-n.tldr: A stability-based analysis of membrane-potential perturbations motivates modified spiking neurons and training that improves robustness in image-classification experiments.

paragraphs: When classification predictions are uncertain, converting them into a ranking raises questions about both stability and fairness. This paper studies ranking functions that map individual predictions to probability distributions over possible rankings. Stability concerns whether small changes in predictions lead to controlled changes in the resulting ranking distribution.

The authors show that deterministic ranking functions cannot provide the studied stability property except in trivial scenarios. Previously proposed uncertainty-aware ranking functions do satisfy it. They also establish that stability composes well with individual fairness, connecting the behavior of the ranking stage to fairness properties of the predictions it receives.

The main result extends this connection to groups: uncertainty-aware rankings achieve group-fairness guarantees when combined with multiaccurate or multicalibrated predictors. Those predictor conditions are part of the guarantee. Together, the findings show how uncertainty-aware ranking can connect individual and group fairness while preserving stability, providing a principled way to carry appropriate prediction-level properties into decisions expressed as rankings.
icml-2024-stability-and-multigroup-fairn.tldr: Uncertainty-aware rankings are stable and can inherit individual and group fairness guarantees from predictors with the appropriate properties.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe alternative scenarios that help reveal which features contributed to a prediction. This paper builds such explanations from semantic graphs accompanying the input, so that relationships between meaningful concepts can enter the explanation. In the visual setting, images are represented as scene graphs rather than only as pixels or isolated concepts.

The method uses a model-agnostic, edit-based approach. To make graph comparisons efficient, it obtains graph-neural-network embeddings for the scene graphs, avoiding the need to solve the NP-hard graph-similarity problem for every input pair. This makes structured semantic information usable within the counterfactual computation while addressing an otherwise expensive comparison step.

Evaluations span benchmark and real-world datasets, different levels of semantic annotation, and diverse classifiers. The explanations outperform previous semantic explanation approaches in quantitative and qualitative comparisons, including human-subject validation. The findings especially emphasize the value of semantic edges when relationships are intricate. The resulting graph-based explanations offer actionable changes while retaining information about how concepts relate to one another.
icml-2024-structure-your-data-towards-se.tldr: Semantic-graph counterfactuals use efficient learned graph comparisons to produce explanations that better capture meaningful relationships and perform well in human evaluations.

paragraphs: An explanation of one model decision may also be useful for nearby inputs, but its reliability across that neighborhood needs assessment. This paper formalizes probabilistic explanation certification for a black-box model accessible only through queries. The inputs are an example, its explanation, and a chosen quality measure such as fidelity or stability.

The problem is to find the largest centered hypercube within which the explanation meets a specified quality criterion with high probability. This region is called a trust region. Framing the task this way turns a single-example explanation into a regional statement, while making the probabilistic nature of the assurance explicit.

The authors propose solutions with computable theoretical guarantees and demonstrate their effectiveness on synthetic and real data. Such regions can support explanation reuse, provide insight into regional model behavior, and establish explanation stability. They may also serve as a measure for comparing explanation methods. The contribution is thus both a certification problem and methods for giving explanations a defined, probabilistically supported scope.
icml-2024-trust-regions-for-explanations.tldr: The paper develops query-based methods to probabilistically certify regions where an existing model explanation satisfies a chosen quality criterion.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on successive tasks, creating the possibility that later learning degrades earlier knowledge. This paper analyzes that forgetting in linear regression trained with stochastic gradient descent. Its theoretical framework covers both under-parameterized and overparameterized regimes, allowing it to study task ordering and algorithmic choices across both settings.

The analysis finds that, when the data size is sufficiently large, placing tasks with larger population-covariance eigenvalues later in the sequence tends to increase forgetting. This connects task order to the statistical structure of the inputs, rather than treating ordering as interchangeable. The direction of the finding is conditional on the stated data-size requirement.

The authors also show that an appropriate step-size choice can help mitigate forgetting in both parameterization regimes. Simulations with linear regression and deep neural networks support the theoretical findings. The work therefore identifies task sequence and step size as interacting factors in forgetting, with formal analysis in linear regression and additional experimental support from the neural-network simulations.
icml-2024-understanding-forgetting-in-co.tldr: Linear-regression theory links forgetting to task order and step size, with sufficiently large datasets revealing greater forgetting when larger-covariance-eigenvalue tasks come later.
